design_rationale: The paper reports a 2-year follow-up of a three-armed randomized controlled trial in which 175 participants were randomly allocated by an independent statistician using variable block sizes and sealed consecutively numbered envelopes (NCT01778972).

domain_judgments.rationale: Allocation sequence was generated by an independent statistician with variable block sizes, concealed in consecutively numbered envelopes handled by staff not involved in data collection or intervention, and baseline characteristics were well balanced across the three arms.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "A statistician independent of the research group generated the random allocation, performed in variable block sizes. The random allocation sequences were transferred to consecutively numbered envelopes and were handled by two researchers who were not involved in the data collection or the intervention."

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and intervention providers were necessarily unblinded, adherence to the prescribed exercise was poor (only 22% met the recommended frequency at 12 months) and exercise behaviour was entirely unmonitored during the second year, and the authors explicitly rejected intention-to-treat analysis, analysing only completers with valid 2-year values.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "This study did not use intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis, which is commonly used in RCT studies. The decision to exclude ITT analysis was made based on the dropout rate being over 10%"

domain_judgments.rationale: Only 124/175 (71%) were followed up, with differential attrition across arms (OEP 62%, OEP+MI 72%, control 79% retained) and analyses restricted to those with valid 2-year values; fall calendars were also incomplete in year 2, and although chi-square tests on a few background factors were non-significant, the loss is large enough and imbalanced enough to threaten the results.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "the OEP group included 38 (62%) of the 61 participants who were included at baseline; the OEP+MI group included 42 participants (72%) of the 58 ...; and the control group included 44 (79%) of the 56 ... Some subjects failed to fill in their fall calendars during the second year."

domain_judgments.rationale: Validated instruments (SPPB, Jamar dynamometer, FES-S, EQ-5D) were applied identically across groups by experienced physiotherapists with the study described as single blinded, but blinding of assessors is not clearly documented for the 2-year wave and key outcomes (falls, physical activity) were self-reported by unblinded participants, with falls partly imputed from recall questionnaires.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "The study was performed single blinded." ... "if available, data on falls were imputed with the corresponding question about fall frequency during the last year from the questionnaire used at the follow-ups."

domain_judgments.rationale: The trial was prospectively registered (NCT01778972) and CONSORT-reported, but the 2-year follow-up analysis plan appears post hoc (the authors note "it was determined that a 2-year follow-up ... would provide some useful information"), multiple outcomes were analysed without correction, and the physical activity scale was dichotomized/analysed in several ways without a pre-specified rule.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "To facilitate analysis of differences between groups in the Frändin–Grimby scale, it was dichotomized between values 2 and 3"

overall_summary: Although randomization and allocation concealment were robust and validated outcome measures were used, the 2-year follow-up is at high risk of bias because of substantial and differentially distributed attrition (29% overall, completers-only analysis with ITT explicitly rejected) combined with unmonitored, largely non-adherent intervention delivery in the second year. These deviation and missing-data problems, plus some concerns about self-reported/imputed outcomes and post hoc analytic choices, drive an overall judgment of high risk.

design_rationale: The paper reports a cluster randomized controlled trial in which participating general practitioners were randomly allocated to the complex exercise intervention or usual care using a blockwise randomization list generated by an independent statistician ("the GPs were randomized either to the intervention or the CG"; "Randomization was conducted by a blockwise randomization list for both coordination centers, by a statistician who was otherwise uninvolved in the study").

domain_judgments.rationale: Although clusters (GPs) were allocated by an independent statistician using a block randomization list, unblinded GPs recruited and enrolled their own patients AFTER cluster allocation, producing a classic identification/recruitment bias in cluster trials; group sizes were markedly unequal (222 vs 156) and some baseline characteristics differed (e.g., walking aids 32.9% vs 43.9%, dizziness 50.2% vs 59.2%), which the authors themselves flag.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Another limitation is that the randomization process of the GPs took place before they started recruiting patients, thus causing a problem with the congruency of every variable, despite clear inclusion criteria."

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants, GPs and staff were all aware of allocation (unavoidable in an exercise trial) and the control group received nothing, so expectancy/motivation effects are plausible; adherence to supervised sessions was high but unsupervised training was self-reported and no explicit intention-to-treat analysis or handling of cluster/participant dropout is described.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Neither the GP nor staff members were blinded to the randomization allocation − blinding for the testing procedure is not feasible in an exercise intervention study"

domain_judgments.rationale: Attrition numbers between T0 and T1 are only shown in an unreadable flow diagram and are not quantified in the text; the authors acknowledge that some randomized GPs dropped out or recruited no patients, and no sensitivity analysis of missingness is reported, although mixed-effects modelling was used.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "In addition, not all randomized GPs were able to recruit participants or lost interest and therefore dropped out the study."

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcomes were assessed by the GPs' own staff who knew the cluster allocation, with stopwatch-timed performance tests susceptible to assessor influence, and the key psychological outcome (FES-I) was self-reported by unblinded participants who knew whether they had received an intervention aimed precisely at reducing fear of falling.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "the eligible patient was tested by the GP or the trained staff member... Neither the GP nor staff members were blinded to the randomization allocation"

domain_judgments.rationale: The trial was registered and the protocol published with no stated changes, and Bonferroni-corrected CIs were used; however, this report covers only the short-term "secondary outcomes" while the pre-specified primary fall outcome is deferred, and the final two-level model specification was selected post hoc after testing the GP level.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "None of the four outcome models showed the third level of GPs as relevant... Hence, two-level models were sufficient to represent the data structure while preserving parsimony."

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high, driven by post-randomization patient recruitment by unblinded GPs (identification/recruitment bias with unequal, partly imbalanced groups) and by outcome measurement performed by unblinded practice staff plus self-reported fear-of-falling in unblinded participants. Incompletely reported attrition and some analytic flexibility add further, lesser concerns.

design_rationale: Explicit cluster randomization: "The 16 senior centers were randomly assigned to one of the four treatment groups (exercise, cognitive-behavioral, exercise-cognitive, discussion control), and all subjects at a center were given the same intervention."

domain_judgments.rationale: Cluster randomization is stated but the sequence-generation method and allocation concealment are not described, participants were recruited at centers after allocation (risk of identification/recruitment bias), and there is a notable gender imbalance across arms.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "For this study, senior centers (rather than individuals) were randomly assigned to treatments." ... "In the exercise and discussion control groups, about 90% were women, compared with about 70% in the other two groups."

domain_judgments.rationale: Primary fall outcomes were nearly complete (survival analysis of 229), but secondary outcomes were available for fewer than half the sample (e.g., balance n = 102 of 230, with very unequal group numbers), and 20% overall attrition with more previous fallers among dropouts (37% vs 27%) raises substantial potential for bias in the reported outcomes.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Physiological and cognitive outcome measures were obtained initially (Time 1) and after 12 months of the intervention programs (Time 2) from a subsample of 112 participants who were available for testing on both occasions."

domain_judgments.rationale: Falls and injury severity were self-reported by unblinded participants to unblinded staff (though weekly contact and diaries mitigate recall bias), and secondary performance tests were presumably administered by non-blinded assessors; blinding of outcome assessors is nowhere described.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Community-based research on falls still must rely on self-reports in documenting falls." ... "Injury severity was based on self-report."

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and instructors necessarily knew their condition (behavioral classes differing in frequency: 3x vs 1x weekly), co-intervention/contamination and non-adherence occurred, and the analysis approach (ITT vs per-protocol) and adjustment for clustering are not clearly reported.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Dropout/noncompliance was defined as missing one-third or more of the classes taught at their center."

domain_judgments.rationale: No pre-registered protocol or analysis plan is available, and although a priori power calculations and primary/secondary outcomes are stated, multiple post hoc outcome operationalizations (injury level thresholds, repeat fallers, extrapolated survival estimates) suggest analytic flexibility.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "In order to compare our faller rate with other studies, we analyzed the rate of falls that entailed injury level 4 or greater..."

overall_summary: Overall high risk of bias, driven by substantial and differential missing outcome data (20% attrition, more prior fallers among dropouts, and secondary outcomes measured in only ~half of participants). Additional concerns arise from undescribed randomization/allocation procedures with baseline gender imbalance, unblinded participants and self-reported outcomes, and the absence of a pre-specified protocol or clustering-adjusted analysis.

design_rationale: The paper explicitly reports a three-arm randomized controlled trial in which "The first author used a computer-developed random table to randomly assign patients to three intervention groups: control, CB alone or CB with Tai Chi."

domain_judgments.rationale: A computer-generated random table was used and allocation was concealed from the recruiting research assistant; baseline demographic, falls-related and outcome variables were well balanced across the three groups (all P > 0.05).
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "The first author used a computer-developed random table to randomly assign patients to three intervention groups... Allocation was concealed from the recruiting RA."

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and intervention providers were necessarily aware of assignment (group CB classes and Tai Chi lessons vs. no extra care), adherence rates to the required sessions are not reported, and the control group received only a brochure with no attention-control, although an intention-to-treat mixed model analysis including all randomized participants was used.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Changes in outcome variables at various follow-up times were predicted using a mixed model approach with an intent-to-treat approach whereby all randomized participants were included"

domain_judgments.rationale: Only 14 of 186 participants (7.5%) withdrew over 5 months, attrition was broadly similar across arms, dropouts and completers were similar at baseline, and a mixed model accounting for missing follow-up data was used.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Of 186 elderly adults recruited for this trial, 14 withdrew during the 5-month study... The dropouts and non-dropouts were similar in baseline data (Table 1)."

domain_judgments.rationale: Validated instruments were used and assessors were reported as blinded, but the principal outcomes are self-reported by unblinded participants (fear of falling, social support, QOL) and blinding of the home-visiting assessor could plausibly have been broken; falls were self-recorded on a checklist.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Participants in all three groups were assessed in their homes for outcomes... by an RA blinded to their group allocation."

domain_judgments.rationale: No trial registration number or published protocol/analysis plan is cited, and multiple outcome operationalizations (two fear-of-falling scales, falls count and rate, several mobility and QOL subscales, multiple time points, ANOVA plus mixed models) were analysed and reported, allowing scope for selective reporting.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Fear of falling was measured by the Geriatric Fear of Falling Measure (GFFM, Huang 2006) and FES (Tinetti et al. 1990)."

overall_summary: Randomization and attrition were handled well (computer-generated allocation with concealment, balanced baselines, <8% dropout, ITT mixed models), but the trial carries some concerns from unavoidable participant awareness of allocation with unreported adherence, reliance on self-reported outcomes in an unblinded behavioural intervention, and the absence of a registered protocol alongside multiple outcome measures and analyses.

design_rationale: The paper describes a cluster-randomized controlled feasibility trial in which 13 senior centers were allocated by coin toss to the SESEP intervention (6 sites) or an attention-control nutrition course (7 sites): "This study used a randomized control design with senior centers randomized... A coin was tossed to determine allocation between the Brooklyn sites and the South Bronx/Upper Manhattan sites."

domain_judgments.rationale: Allocation was effectively a single coin toss assigning entire geographic regions, so intervention status is fully confounded with borough/neighbourhood characteristics and there was no meaningful concealed sequence; participants were also recruited and consented after cluster allocation (risk of differential recruitment), with notably unequal group sizes (100 vs 66), although measured baseline demographics and outcomes did not differ.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Sites were randomized by geographic cluster (Brooklyn or South Bronx/Upper Manhattan) in order to prevent contamination... A coin was tossed to determine allocation between the Brooklyn sites and the South Bronx/Upper Manhattan sites."

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and lay interventionists necessarily knew the assigned condition (an attention-control nutrition class was used to mitigate this), but fidelity/exposure was poorly documented, attendance was not recorded at control sites, and the analysis appears to be of available cases rather than a clearly specified intention-to-treat analysis.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "While the numbers of participants at each SESEP class were collected, the individual names of attendees were not consistently recorded. In addition, it was not known how much time the individual actually engaged in exercise during the class... Attendance was not kept at the control sites."

domain_judgments.rationale: 38% of participants had no follow-up data, loss was differential by arm (64% retained in intervention vs 59% in control, with follow-up occurring on a single testing day and no attempt to contact absentees), and the reasons for missingness are unknown — which the authors themselves state "certainly can bias the findings."
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Follow-up testing included 103 participants (62%), 39 from control sites and 64 from treatment sites... There was a significant loss to follow-up with no information obtained as to why the participant did not attend the follow-up screening."

domain_judgments.rationale: Primary outcomes (self-efficacy, outcome expectations, exercise time, physical activity) were self-reported by unblinded participants via interviewer-administered surveys, the efficacy-enhancing intervention explicitly taught the content of the outcome-expectation measure (risk of response bias), and performance measures (Tinetti, chair rise) were assessed by staff with no stated blinding.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "the outcomes were all based on self-report rather than objective measures of physical activity (e.g., actigraphy)"

domain_judgments.rationale: No protocol or trial registration is cited and no power analysis was done, but two hypotheses with pre-specified primary and secondary outcome sets were stated a priori and all 11 outcomes (including null results) are reported in full, which limits concern about selective reporting; clustering was nonetheless tested post hoc and then ignored in the analysis.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Given that this was a feasibility study and involved pilot testing of the SESEP, no a priori power analysis was performed."

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high, driven by a single coin-toss cluster allocation that confounded intervention with geographic area (with post-randomization recruitment and unequal arm sizes), substantial and unexplained differential loss to follow-up (only 62% retained, reasons unknown), and reliance on self-reported outcomes from unblinded participants whose intervention directly addressed the measured constructs. Concerns about intervention fidelity/exposure documentation, unaccounted clustering, and absence of a registered protocol or power analysis compound these problems.

design_rationale: The paper explicitly describes a prospective two-group randomized controlled trial with stratification by race and living arrangement and allocation via random permuted blocks and opaque envelopes.

domain_judgments.rationale: Allocation used stratified random permuted blocks with the block size concealed from staff and double opaque envelopes, and Table 1 shows baseline characteristics balanced across groups (all P>.15).
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Study participants were stratified by race (white, nonwhite) and living arrangement (alone, with others) and randomized within each of four strata using random permuted blocks... The blocking number, developed by the project statistician (WWH), remained unknown to others. Randomization lists and four sets of randomization were prepared using double, opaque envelopes."

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and interventionists necessarily knew the assignment and the comparator was a no-treatment control (no attention control), so performance/expectancy effects could influence the largely self-reported outcomes, although fidelity was monitored and an intention-to-treat analysis was used.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "One potential limitation of this study was the use of a no-treatment control group, which leaves open the possibility that attention from health professionals may account for the beneficial effects"

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome data were available for 94% at 6 months and 89% at 12 months, with reasons for discontinuation documented (mostly death/illness) and unlikely to depend on true outcome values.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Of the 319 participants (159 control, 160 experimental), 300 (94%) were available at 6 months and 285 (89%) at 12 months."

domain_judgments.rationale: Interviewers were masked to allocation and standardized instruments were used, but the primary outcomes were participant self-reports from unblinded participants (one measure investigator-developed with modest reliability, α=0.58–0.69), and no objective performance-based measures were included.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "A related concern is that the primary study outcomes were subjective self-reports of difficulty with daily life tasks and that performance-based measures were not included."

domain_judgments.rationale: Primary/secondary outcomes, covariates and power assumptions were pre-specified a priori, but no trial registration/protocol is cited, multiple outcomes plus item-level subanalyses are reported, and the stated analysis plan (one-sided α=0.0167 for three primary endpoints) differs from the reported two-sided α=.05 tests, suggesting some analytic flexibility.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "An a 5 0.05/3 5 0.0167 level, one-sided test, was used... with significance level set at .05 (SPSS, Inc., Chicago, IL). All analyses were two-sided."

overall_summary: Randomization and retention were well handled, but the trial used an unblinded no-treatment (non-attention) control with predominantly self-reported primary outcomes, and the reported significance thresholds deviate from the pre-specified analysis plan without an available protocol/registration. These concerns in D2, D4 and D5 yield an overall judgment of some concerns.

design_rationale: Explicit computer-generated block randomization of 540 participants to a cognitive behavioral group intervention or usual care, with a registered parallel-group RCT protocol (ISRCTN43792817).

domain_judgments.rationale: Computer-generated block randomization performed after baseline measurement by an independent researcher blinded to participant characteristics, with baseline characteristics comparable between groups.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "After baseline measurement, an independent researcher blinded to participant characteristics performed block randomization (two communities 5 cycles) using a computer-generated random allocation (SPSS 12.0)"

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants were necessarily unblinded and intervention uptake/adherence was poor (42.1% attended fewer than five sessions, 72 withdrew before starting), though no crossover occurred and a modified intention-to-treat analysis was used, so the deviations largely reflect usual implementation rather than analysis bias.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Participants were not blinded to group assignment. No participant assigned to the intervention group crossed over to the control group or vice versa."; "One hundred sixty-two participants (57.9%) attended at least five sessions, and 118 (42.1%) attended fewer than five sessions"

domain_judgments.rationale: 25% overall loss to follow-up with differential attrition (30.0% intervention vs 19.6% control) and self-reported outcomes that could plausibly relate to the outcome itself; mitigated by MCAR testing, similar dropout reasons, no baseline differences between dropouts, mixed-effects models and sensitivity multiple imputation.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "During the trial, 135 participants were lost to follow-up: 51 (19.6%) of the control group and 84 (30.0%) of the intervention group."

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome assessors were trained and blinded and measures were validated and applied identically, but the primary outcomes are self-reported by unblinded participants in an unmasked behavioral/psychological intervention, which can inflate subjective reports (e.g., the very large OR 0.11 for fear of falling).
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Outcome assessors were trained centrally on study procedures and were blind to group assignment."

domain_judgments.rationale: The trial was registered (ISRCTN43792817) with a published design/protocol paper, the analysis adjustments and per-protocol analyses were pre-specified a priori, and all outcomes at all three follow-ups (including null results) are reported.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "A priori it was specified that all models would be adjusted for baseline values, age, sex, living situation, educational level, cognitive status, perceived general health, and falls history at baseline."

overall_summary: Allocation and reporting were robust (concealed computer-generated randomization, registered protocol, pre-specified analyses), but some concerns arise from unblinded participants with low intervention uptake/adherence, differential loss to follow-up (30% vs 20%), and reliance on self-reported subjective outcomes in an unmasked behavioral trial. No domain reached high risk, so the overall judgment is 'some concerns'.

design_rationale: The paper describes a "single-blinded, four-group, randomized controlled trial" in which participants were allocated by a third party using a computerized random-number generator with concealed allocation.

domain_judgments.rationale: Although the sequence was computer-generated and concealed, randomization occurred separately within two recruitment waves so that the control group was randomized only against the multifaceted group; the headline SBG/FG versus control comparisons are therefore between-wave, non-randomized contrasts, and baseline imbalances in education (P = .04) and fear of falling (P = .02) were observed.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "These people were randomly assigned to the CG (n = 80) or MG (n = 73). People recruited in Wave 2 (n = 1,000) were similarly addressed... randomly assigned to the SBG (n = 63) or FG (n = 64). All randomizations were concealed. (A third party not involved in the study applied a computerized random-number generator.)"

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants necessarily knew their allocation and controls received no attention-matched comparator (risking performance/expectation effects, especially for self-reported psychological outcomes), although adherence was high (~82–84% attended ≥24/32 sessions), fidelity was monitored, and a modified ITT analysis was used.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "The CG received no intervention as part of this study." / "All analyses were performed according to a modified intention-to-treat design (i.e., all baseline data and available follow-up data were included)."

domain_judgments.rationale: About a quarter of participants (73 lost to follow-up) lacked complete 24-month data and no imputation or sensitivity analysis was performed beyond reliance on mixed models, though dropout appeared unrelated to key baseline characteristics.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Complete data sets were available for 207 participants (73.9%) for 24 months, and data were missing... for 47 persons (16.8%) at 24 months." / "Post hoc analyses showed no significant baseline differences (P < .05) in age, sex, or number of participants that had fallen in the past 6 months regarding dropout in all groups."

domain_judgments.rationale: Physical performance was measured with validated tests by blinded assessors, but the fall-related psychological outcomes and falls were self-reported by unblinded participants, and balance confidence lacked a baseline measurement.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "The assessors administering the physical performance tests received training and were blinded to group assignment." / "Balance confidence was assessed at follow-up only."

domain_judgments.rationale: No trial registration or protocol is cited and many outcomes (9 measures × 3 time points × 3 group contrasts) were tested without adjustment for multiplicity, so selective emphasis of significant findings cannot be excluded, although covariate adjustment was stated to be pre-specified.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Adjustment of the models for available baseline values of the outcome variables age, sex, living situation, education, fear of falling, and having fallen in the past 6 months was specified a priori."

overall_summary: Overall high risk of bias, driven by the randomization domain: allocation was computer-generated and concealed but performed within two separate recruitment waves, so the principal SBG/FG-versus-control comparisons are not truly randomized contrasts and baseline imbalances in education and fear of falling were present. Additional 'some concerns' arise from unblinded participants with a no-intervention control, ~26% attrition by 24 months, self-reported psychological/falls outcomes, and absence of a registered protocol with many multiplicity-untested outcomes.

design_rationale: Participants were allocated to ABLE or fall prevention education using an explicit random allocation procedure: "Randomization was determined using a computer-generated sequence created and held by a colleague with no other connection to the study," with 21 participants randomized per arm and a CONSORT diagram and trial registration (NCT01609322).

domain_judgments.rationale: Sequence generation and allocation concealment were adequate, but several prognostically relevant baseline imbalances (psychiatric diagnosis, depression, specific phobia, p=.01–.04) occurred and the authors themselves state these "may have biased our findings in favor of the ABLE intervention," so some concerns remain despite plausible chance imbalance in a small pilot.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Randomization was determined using a computer-generated sequence created and held by a colleague with no other connection to the study; the project coordinator obtained the assignment after each participant completed the baseline assessment." ... "participants assigned to ABLE were more likely to meet criteria for a psychiatric disorder overall or a past or current history of major depression, and participants assigned to FPE were more likely to meet criteria for specific phobia"

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and interventionists were necessarily aware of assignment and the control arm may have recognized its intervention did not target fear (with differential credibility ratings, p=.05), though fidelity was monitored by videotape review and an appropriate intention-to-treat analysis was used.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "It is also possible that our frequent assessment of fear of falling may have biased the results, as individuals receiving FPE may have become aware that their intervention was not targeting fear directly." ... "Intention-to-treat analyses were conducted using repeated measures mixed effects models"

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome data were available for 40/42 (95%) participants, attrition was minimal and nearly balanced in impact, and mixed-effects models retained all available observations.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Two participants dropped out of ABLE (9.5%) after 4 weeks. A total of 40 participants completed treatment and follow-up." ... "Models were assessed using the MIXED procedure which does not use listwise deletion and thus preserves degrees of freedom in the presence of missing data."

domain_judgments.rationale: Both primary outcomes were subjective self-reports from unblinded participants (assessor blinding does not remove participant-report bias, and the authors acknowledge the repeated fear assessments may have cued control participants), and the avoidance measure was an unvalidated ad hoc modification of the Activity Card Sort.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "The primary outcome measures were fear of falling and activity avoidance due to fear." ... "For purposes of this study, we modified the original measure to include additional cards representing common activities that are often avoided due to fear of falling"

domain_judgments.rationale: The trial was prospectively registered (NCT01609322) with clearly stated primary outcomes, but no protocol/analysis plan is cited, covariates were evidently added post hoc to adjust for observed baseline imbalances, the avoidance outcome was customized, and many simple-effects tests across multiple time points were reported without adjustment.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "All models included credibility scores and presence or absence of a psychiatric disorder as covariates to control for group differences on these variables."

overall_summary: Overall high risk of bias, driven by D4: both primary outcomes (FES-I fear of falling and a study-modified Activity Card Sort) were subjective self-reports from participants who were necessarily aware of their assigned condition, with the authors noting that frequent fear assessments may have signalled to control participants that their program did not target fear. Additional some-concerns arose from baseline psychiatric imbalances favouring ABLE (acknowledged by the authors as potentially biasing), unblinded delivery, and post hoc covariate adjustment/multiple time-point testing in this small pilot trial.

design_rationale: Participants were explicitly randomised to three arms using a predetermined randomisation list prepared by an independent statistician with variable block sizes: "After baseline assessments were completed, the participants were randomised to one of the three groups... Randomisation was performed in blocks... with a variable size of three, six, nine or twelve participants."

domain_judgments.rationale: An independent statistician generated a predetermined, variable-block randomisation list, allocation was performed by an independent physiotherapist after baseline assessment, and baseline characteristics did not differ significantly between the three arms.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "A predetermined randomisation list was made by an independent statistician. Randomisation was performed in blocks to minimise the risk of revealing treatment group membership, with a variable size of three, six, nine or twelve participants." / "There were no significant baseline differences between the three groups (Table 1)."

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and treating physiotherapists were necessarily aware of allocation, exercise was carried out as planned in only 73% of cases, the MI guide was judged insufficient (fidelity shortfall), and the effect analyses appear to be available-case/per-protocol rather than intention-to-treat.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Exercises that were performed as planned were rated as ‘yes’ in 73% of the questionnaires" / "At the beginning of the study, an MI guide was used but was found to be insufficient for the PTs performing the MI."

domain_judgments.rationale: Five of 45 randomised participants (11%) lacked 3-month follow-up and outcome tables report only 13–14 per group with no analysis of reasons for, or impact of, missingness.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Three-month follow-ups were conducted for 40 participants."

domain_judgments.rationale: Validated, reliable instruments (Mini-BESTest, SPPB, FES(S)) were applied identically across arms by an independent physiotherapist blinded to allocation; falls were self-reported via standard calendars, a minor but non-differential limitation.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "All measurements were completed in the participant's home or at a health care centre formed by an independent PT who was blinded for group randomisation."

domain_judgments.rationale: No trial registration or pre-specified analysis plan is cited for this feasibility report, multiple outcomes and both between- and within-group analyses were conducted, and the narrative emphasises selective within-group significant findings in an underpowered sample.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "The FES(S) was only significantly improved over time in the MI group (p = 0.02, ES (r) = 0.45), which possibly reflects an important effect of MI treatment."

overall_summary: Randomisation and blinded outcome assessment were well handled, but unblinded participants/therapists with documented fidelity shortfalls (MI guide insufficient; exercise as planned in only 73%), 11% loss to follow-up without missingness analysis, and absence of a pre-specified protocol/registration with emphasis on selective within-group results raise concerns. No domain reached high risk, so the overall judgment is some concerns.

design_rationale: Explicit parallel-group RCT: participants were randomly allocated by an independent statistician using variable block sizes stratified by community, with sequences in consecutively numbered envelopes; registered at clinicaltrials.gov (NCT01778972).

domain_judgments.rationale: Sequence generated by an independent statistician with variable block sizes stratified by community, concealed in consecutively numbered envelopes handled by researchers not involved in data collection or intervention, and baseline characteristics showed no significant between-group differences.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "The participants were randomly allocated in variable block sizes of 3, 6, 9, and 12 participants to 1 of 3 groups. The randomization was stratified by the 3 communities. A statistician independent from the research group generated the random allocation. The random allocation sequences were transferred to consecutively numbered envelopes that were handled by 2 researchers who did not participate in the data collection or in the intervention."

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and delivering physiotherapists necessarily knew allocation (unblindable behavioral/exercise intervention), the control group received only a pamphlet and no diary so co-intervention/self-exercise is unknown (authors note an "unexpected improvement in the control group"), and OEP vs OEP+MI contrast may have been blurred since all PTs were MI-experienced; however, treatment fidelity was monitored and an intention-to-treat analysis was performed.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "The control group did not keep exercise diaries, so it is unknown whether this group exercised on their own." ... "All of the PTs who performed the MI had received education in MI, and they were all experienced and familiar with the MI method."

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome data were available for 161/175 (92%) participants, dropouts were few and fairly balanced (7 OEP, 6 OEP+MI, 1 control) and attributed mainly to health problems unlikely to differ systematically in a way that would bias the null result; a per-protocol analysis gave similar results to the ITT analysis.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "A total of 161 participants were followed up at 12 weeks: 54 individuals in the OEP group, 52 individuals in the OEP + MI group, and 55 individuals in the control group... The 14 dropouts during the study period were mostly due to participants' health-related problems."

domain_judgments.rationale: Primary and secondary outcomes used validated, reliable instruments administered identically by assessors blinded to allocation, but several outcomes are self-reported by unblinded participants (Falls Efficacy Scale, Frändin/Grimby activity scale, fall calendar, exercise diary—absent in controls), which leaves scope for reporting bias; blinding success was also not verified.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "The measurements were performed single blinded by 6 independent PTs before randomization and 12 weeks after randomization." ... "In addition, the PTs who performed the measurements were blinded to group allocation"

domain_judgments.rationale: The trial was prospectively registered (NCT01778972) with a pre-specified primary outcome (SPPB) and a priori power calculation, and both ITT and per-protocol analyses are reported; however, the registry protocol is not compared in detail, multiple outcomes/time points exist, and emphasis in the abstract/discussion on uncorrected within-group significance tests (not the pre-specified between-group comparison) suggests selective emphasis of favorable analyses without adjustment for multiplicity.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Within the OEP + MI group, physical performance, fall self-efficacy, physical activity level, and handgrip strength improved significantly" ... "A power calculation based on the SPPB, the main outcome variable, was performed before the study started."

overall_summary: Randomization and attrition were well handled (independent statistician, concealed envelopes, balanced baselines, 92% follow-up, blinded assessors), but the trial carries some concerns from the inherently unblinded exercise/MI intervention with an un-monitored control group, partly self-reported outcomes, and emphasis on unadjusted within-group analyses rather than the pre-specified between-group comparison. No domain reached high risk, so the overall judgment is "some concerns"; the headline finding of no between-group differences is nonetheless vulnerable to the acknowledged underpowering and short 12-week follow-up.

design_rationale: Explicit two-group randomized controlled trial with computerized stratified block randomization performed by an external agency after baseline measurement (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01358032).

domain_judgments.rationale: Computer-generated stratified randomization executed by an independent external agency after baseline assessment ensures concealed allocation, and the reported baseline characteristics were well balanced (all p > .10).
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "A computerized two-block randomization was performed using the level of concerns about falls... An external agency blinded to participant characteristics conducted the randomization directly after the baseline measurement."

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and facilitators were necessarily unblinded and there was substantial non-adherence (15% never started; 29% of starters withdrew; 'exposure in vivo' performed by only half), although an appropriate intention-to-treat analysis based on original allocation was used, limiting the impact.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Thirty participants in the intervention group (15 %) were not exposed to the program; they withdrew from the intervention prior to the first session. Among the people who started the program, 29 % (47 out of 164) withdrew."

domain_judgments.rationale: Loss to follow-up was large and markedly differential by arm (17% vs 31–34%, with withdrawal highest immediately after the intervention period and reasons including 'lost interest' and health problems that plausibly relate to the outcome), and although the authors report no significant baseline differences between completers and dropouts, this cannot exclude outcome-related missingness.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "dropout of study participants was substantial and different in both groups, i.e. 17 % in the control group and 34 % in the intervention group. Therefore selective dropout may be an issue"

domain_judgments.rationale: Validated instruments (FES-I, GARS, prospective fall calendars) were used identically in both arms with blinded assessors, but the primary outcome is participant self-report and participants knew their allocation, so reporting could have been influenced by expectations.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Facilitators and participants were aware of group assignments; outcome assessors were blinded to the allocation."

domain_judgments.rationale: The trial was prospectively registered with a published a priori protocol specifying primary/secondary outcomes, covariates, one-tailed testing and pre-planned per-protocol analyses, and all specified outcomes (including null findings for total falls) are reported.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Additional information about the study design can be found in a published study protocol [24]." ... "Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT01358032."

overall_summary: Allocation and reporting were methodologically strong (concealed computerized stratified randomization by an external agency, pre-registered protocol, ITT analysis with blinded assessors), but substantial and differentially distributed attrition (17% control vs 31–34% intervention, largely immediately post-intervention) drives a high risk of bias for missing outcome data, compounded by unblinded participants reporting the self-report primary outcome.
